A precise determination of the B^0_s meson's lifetime is crucial, given the particle's unique combination of heavy flavor and light strangeness.  One particularly interesting aspect of this measurement involves the semi-leptonic decay mode, which is less受中性的 B^0_s meson衰变宽度主导的衰变模式. 为了获得最准确的 B^0_s 半轻子衰变宽度, 我们需要理解强子形式因子, 特别是在零反冲点, 其中拉格朗日通用化理论提供了最有价值的见解. 然而, 形成因子与矩阵元之间的转换对于新的物理现象的研究至关重要, 这使得该主题对于超越标准模型的探索极具相关性.

This study aims to resolve a specific class of stochastic control problems where we seek to understand the behavior of systems influenced by multiple sources of randomness as they occur over brief time periods. Various research efforts have offered different methods, including discrete approximation techniques, whose effectiveness relies on establishing sufficient conditions for the value function's uniqueness. This research presents an innovative solution by applying the stochastic Perron method to prove that, under certain conditions, classical approximation algorithms successfully achieve desired outcomes even when systems involve significant fluctuations caused by strong randomness.

Our analysis of dipole anisotropy in cosmic ray directions divides the sky into two hemispheres based on dipole latitude.
We compare the mean energy in each hemisphere and investigate the relationship between energy and dipole anisotropy amplitude in different energy ranges.
Using the complete dataset from 2009 to 2019, we observe a significant increase in anisotropy above 4 EeV.
However, above EeV energies we find the anisotropy amplitude to be 7.4% with no significant magnetic deflection between the two ranges.
This increased anisotropy amplitude suggests a possible change in the most influential massive cluster in that energy range.

This correlation poses critical questions regarding $R_{pp}$'s applicability as an indicator of the centrality-dependent size or density of the quark-gluon plasma. To investigate this, a correlation between the centrality of collisions and a $J/\psi$-based quantity, denoted as $R_{MGF}$, which is independent of the probability distribution function for $P_{T}$ and less influenced by initial state effects, has been measured in $Pb-Pb$ and proton-lead ($p-Pb$) collisions at 2.76 TeV, and data from lone $p-p$ collisions with equivalent center-of-mass energy. The findings indicate that $R_{p p}$ is not constant across $p-p$ collisions, and more importantly, the variation of $R_{p p}$ across collision centrality is largely compensated and opposed by the centrality-dependent variation of $R_{p p}$'s baseline in $p-p$ collisions. In this investigation, we identify differential operators in noncommutative quantum mechanics that correspond to a commuting momentum space, whose operators are multiplicative. These operators in noncommutative mechanics are essentially Heisenberg algebra generators in their classical counterparts. Our derived relations between the noncommutative parameters of the phase space and the deformation parameter of the Heisenberg algebra reveal a connection to the complex geometry of the deformed disc in spectral theory.

The primary objective of this project is to develop a user-friendly tool for non-experts to accurately identify tumor infiltrating lymphocytes on converted histological samples. Lymphocytes play a crucial role in the immune system's ability to combat viruses and tumors, and their behavior can influence patient prognosis on various cancer types. The proposed solution involves using modified object detection and classification algorithms to generate a list of potential lymphocyte locations, which users can then visually verify and mark as positive or negative. Furthermore, an underlying review algorithm will refine these user markings to achieve high accuracy with minimal input from users. So far, baseline versions of two different algorithms have been tested on datasets consisting of converted tumor tissue samples, demonstrating an average precision of 0.735 when only four examples per image were presented to train the refinement model. The project will use crowdsourcing to gather user inputs and test the effectiveness of the proposed solution, ultimately resulting in a user-friendly tool for task analysis.

A new optical equalization technique, the Joint Decision-Feedback Equalization algorithm, is effectively managed at high rates (greater than 40 Gb/s) and demonstrates suitability for correcting multiple-bit error bursts in optical communications. To enhance its decision-feedback capability across multiple error bursts, an optimized sequence is introduced, allowing the MLSE decoder to recover more symbols than the usual FFE+TDFE method. When integrated with appropriate MLSE decoding thresholds, simulation results show significant improvements in system performance, with gains of up to 3.5 dB at a 2% BER rate compared to the conventional FFE+TDFE approach for decision-feedback restoration.

Recently, fully utilizing a graph's topological structure has gained significance by enabling more efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) through techniques like skipping connections and reduced message passing. Although recent works have achieved notable success using GNNs with extreme dilation patterns (EPs), they necessitate extensive EP hyperparameter searches, resulting in time and resource-consuming processes. To address this challenge, we propose a novel End-to-End trainable automatic dilation optimizer (END-OPT) that learns optimal EPs for graph neural networks in an unsupervised manner. Specifically, our method learns EXTEND blocks that can be extremally dilated and applied anywhere in a GNN network to optimize downstream tasks in an end-to-end manner without requiring EP hyperparameter searches. Notably, our EXTEND blocks utilize local and non-local skip-like and message-like operations, allowing for efficient graph neural networks by utilizing a GNN's topological structure with reduced message passing. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of END-OPT, yielding up to 13.7% fewer parameters, 19.2% less GPU memory usage, and up to 1.5 times less inference time compared to the baselines on multiple datasets and EP benchmarks. The optimizer's code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengzhu99/END-OPT.

This paper provides a comprehensive investigation into the finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras that possess a Z_2-grading. Specifically, we examine key properties such as nilpotency, solvability, and Engel conditions in the context of graded structures. Our study includes determination of lower nilpotency, solvability, and Engel lengths for graded associative algebras, Lie algebras, and non-associative non-Lie Zinbiel algebras. Additionally, we establish finite nilpotency, solvability, and Engel properties for certain classes of graded alternative algebras and Jordan algebras. Moreover, we precisely identify the Engel lengths for ternary nilpotent algebras and Jordan pairs. This work extends and builds upon existing research by various authors.

Fluctuations in flow patterns provide valuable insights into the non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma formed during heavy-ion collisions, particularly in relation to initial spatial fluctuations and thermal fluctuations. Furthermore, flow fluctuations serve as an essential tool for distinguishing between different collision scenarios, including proton-lead, nucleus-gold, and gold-gold collisions. This paper examines the coefficients of flow fluctuations across various particles in p-Pb and nAu collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, utilizing data collected by the ALICE detector between 2018 and 2019. Noise reduction techniques are employed to enhance measurement precision, and the results reveal distinct differences between collisions with the nucleus in beam and proton beam directions, particularly evident in elliptic flow differences and flow noise differences for all measured particles. Observed trends in flow fluctuations across transverse momentum ranges offer valuable insights for theoretical modeling.

We extend our previous research by focusing on (D)LE-inductive formulas and thoroughly analyzing their first-order correspondents, with an emphasis on those for modality $\nu$. To efficiently determine these correspondents, the computation building on the method of ALBA is applied. This ALBA-based approach allows for the identification of key steps that allow the ALBA algorithm to successfully compute the first-order correspondents. Additionally, we provide a concise overview of ALBA for (D)LE-formulas and analyze the impact of ALBA extensions when dealing with inductive formulas. Furthermore, we revisit our earlier findings and provide a more in-depth treatment for the modalities $\nu$ and $\boxplus$. This expanded treatment includes considerations for their adjoints, specifically $\rho$ and $\delta$, thereby completing our earlier research for the non-distributive inductive formulas.

This paper explores first-order logic within a four-valued semantic framework, specifically the Kleishlark strong bi-valuation system. We provide a clear explanation of this framework and investigate its application to database theory, particularly in terms of defining and ensuring consistent answers to queries using source databases that may provide unreliable information. Our main contribution is an algorithm that efficiently determines the true answers to first-order logic queries, even when the source database values can be false or both true and false. Our method builds on the framework established in a previous work, but with significant differences due to the four-valued semantic framework. We provide an illustrative example to highlight these differences and show how our algorithm can be applied to safety-of-answers and union of conjunctive queries. Our new method relies on finding a specific model, which can be derived from source views, that helps ensure the queries have true answers. This model is characterized by a set of variables, and its use allows us to efficiently compute the queries' answers by dividing the domain into regions and analyzing each region's properties. This approach offers a more practical and scalable way of ensuring consistent query answers, particularly for large databases.

We introduce a novel linear dynamic model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX), which accommodates non-linear patterns, frequent adjustments, and sudden shifts often observed in high-quality real-time data such as Internet traffic and telecommunication traffic. Leveraging online regression techniques, we provide efficient estimators for time-changing and fixed parameters of the TV-PARX model. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees for the consistency of our estimators under mild assumptions. To illustrate the flexibility and effectiveness of TV-PARX in modeling complex, non-linear time-series, we present a real-world application and compare its performance to that of established alternative models.

To train robust contact-descriptor fields that enable effective manipulation,
little demonstration data is necessary.  By formulating Neural Descriptor Fields
(NDFs), we represent object contacts in 3D space and link them to task-specific
descriptors in a low-dimensional field.  A single narrow field can be trained to
associate contacts with task-relevant features, proving useful across diverse
object shapes and types.  In this work, we investigate training this descriptor
field for whole-arm manipulation tasks using visual-control policies trained via
variant demonstrations in a simulated environment.  We show that learning the
NDF from just a few demonstrations on select object shapes allows successful
generalization to unseen shapes.  Experiments reveal that training data from a
single shape often yields good results, but performance improves significantly
when contacts on different shapes are included.  Additionally, we show that the
NDF generalizes well to tasks never seen during training.

The SiD Detector is a comprehensive detection system designed for the future International Linear Collider's $e^+e^-$ collisions at high precision levels. Its calorimeter system comprises two main components: the SiD ECAL consisting of 14880 lead glass crystals for measuring electromagnetic interactions, and the SiD HCAL made up of steel-scintillator haptares to detect high-energy hadrons. This research utilizes a simulated scenario involving one trillion processed events from mid-range collider operations, specifically ILCS references 1a and 2, to evaluate the performance of the SiD Detector's calorimeter. The calculated jet energy resolution indicates an impressive 1.7% accuracy at 100 GeV and 1.0% at 1 TeV, demonstrating the system's capability to precisely measure high-energy hadrons.

We've created a new high-resolution spectrum for the globular cluster Tononzintla 2, which is located in the Galactic Bulge, through a comprehensive spectral synthesis approach. Using this dataset, we were able to accurately derive the metallicity and various elemental abundances such as oxygen, magnesium, aluminum, silicon, and others from the spectrum. 

Analysis of the spectrum revealed that Tononzintla 2 is relatively metal poor with a metallicity of -0.19 and a moderate spread in elemental abundances with a metallicity to total metal ratio of 0.71. However, it stands out due to an unusually low [Mg/Fe] ratio of approximately 0.3, which is significantly lower than the typical range of 0.7 to 1 unit unit above the solar value units found in similar high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters. 

Our study suggests that the distinct chemical composition of Tononzintla 2 may be a result of the survival of a small, chemically distinct population within the globular cluster as the more massive stars have since evolved and died off.

Researchers who work with interactive theorem proving systems often share their formal proofs within communities, but as proofs become more complex, the underlying dependencies in these proof documents start to mirror scale-free patterns. This poses a challenge for the scalability of these documentation sets. In an effort to address this challenge, we have identified and studied a diverse range of strategies that have been successfully applied to maintain simple node connections in the documentation graphs. Our findings provide a valuable resource for others seeking to create formal proof documentation that is both rigorous and easily shareable.

Building on previous research that reexamined the critical behavior of QCD in three dimensions, this study extends the analysis to include a non-zero theta angle, also known as the axial angle. By expanding the relevant potential function, the critical point has been identified as the point at which the symmetry of the potential breaks, or as an alternative, by utilizing the potential function's anharmonic ratio. The presence of the axial angle results in a shift in the critical point, which can be estimated using a semi-analytical method, provided the angle is not too large. Theoretical predictions are then compared to the results obtained from lattice simulations, with the findings showing that for a specific set of conditions, the critical point occurs at a specific value of the angle, while for a higher set of conditions, the behavior of the system is described as being in the deep Seiberg duality phase, with no indication of chiral symmetry breaking.

We investigate the connection between the Parisi formula and the success of the approximate message-passing (AMP) in recovering a hidden signal from randomized pairwise correlations, a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-synchronization problem. Focusing on this specific type of correlation, we establish a equivalence between the non-convergence of AMP and the strict non-differentiability of the TAP free energy, while the convergence of AMP implies the differentiability of the TAP free energy. Notably, for certain angles less than a critical angle of approximately $0.56$ radians, the TAP formula indicates that full recovery is achievable even though AMP fails to converge in this angle range.

Advanced metasurfaces can be effectively designed and configured using Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions, which provide a crucial electromagnetic relationship between surface electric and magnetic fields in a simplified form. This paper presents an alternative derivation of GSTCs, specifically for atomic-thin chemical compounds, which serves as a testament to their reliability. The GSTC derivation utilizes a basic quantum mechanical approach, deriving the changes in energy within a minuscule volume encompassing a singular molecule situated on a surface. Within this context, constraints are effectively applied using the principles of electromagnetic field behavior and molecular resonance. The resulting GSTC derivation offers a more in-depth understanding of how these conditions arise, specifically focusing on the unique properties of chemical compounds at the subwavelength scale and their relation to electromagnetic wave propagation.

In this study, we investigate several aspects of orbital linearization for systems undergoing blowing-up transformations, specifically hyperbolic and elliptic cases. We prove several key results regarding orbital linearization, including new findings on orbital linearization in elliptic regions. Our proofs rely heavily on the blowing-up method, alongside standard techniques from orbital normalization. Notably, our main contribution lies in establishing foundational tools for orbital linearization by analyzing the orbital blow-up map and introducing orbital stars. We demonstrate how these concepts can be applied to prove the aforementioned results and provide insights into their relationships. Finally, we illustrate one of our methods using an example from previous literature.

We introduce double-variational eCPNN, a novel neural network based on encoder-decoder architecture, which serves as an improved model to compare with base eCPNN. The encoder utilizes multiple neural network layers, comprising affine normalization and residual connections, to create potential functions. These functions, which can be written as $U_\mathrm{enc}$, effectively describe the intricate electron correlations in space through external input currents. The decoder, consisting of $F_\mathrm{dec}$, then generates an optimized external electric field that can be idealized as $E_\mathrm{dec}$$. When applying the model to two-dimensional hydrogen-like electrons subject to strong external magnetic fields, we discover that double-variariant eCPNN展现出 superior performance in model capacity, outperforming both the original eCPNN model and traditional methods such as Monte Carlo simulations.

Recently, researchers using Sloan Digital Sky Survey data have identified a massive structure within the Sloan Digital Sky Survey survey, dubbed the "Great Arc." To understand its true scale, we employed an approach that accounts for distance measurement uncertainties and sample limitations. Our statistical analysis revealed that the Big Arc contains an excess of galaxy counts, with an associated uncertainty of approximately 1-sigma, residing within an 180-Mpc arc. Notably, its shape aligns with the line of sight for redshift-space distortions. When not constrained by these considerations, the overabundance of galaxies becomes less pronounced, affecting regions up to 150 Mpc. Among existing structures discovered using SDSS data, the Big Arc stands out as the most substantial. It contains roughly 1.5 times more galaxies than anticipated by the standard model, with an associated uncertainty of 0.3 times. Notably, the Big Arc exhibits notable correlations with the Sloan Great Wall and the Perseus-Pegasus Wall in real-space power spectrum analysis. However, these correlations fall within the 0.4-$\sigma$ range. It's worth mentioning that the Big Arc spans an extensive 150-Mpc arc and may partially be an artifact arising from the intersection of two 3-D sheet-like structures whose orientations are perpendicular to each other and to the line of sight.

Researchers agree that accurately measuring infrared temperatures is hindered by the uncertainty in the radiometers' sensitivity to the Earth's surface and how much they reflect the atmosphere's radiation. However, an alternative approach to estimating the atmosphere's properties, specifically the amount of scattered light due to particles in the air, has been developed. This new method utilizes wide-angle photography that captures the Earth's radiated energy across a broad field of view, typically from 50 to 80 degrees. By analyzing the radiative balance between the Earth's radiation and the absorption of that radiation across multiple points in the sky, this technique can be calibrated relatively and is not hindered by the instrument's inability to accurately measure the Earth's radiation. This calculation essentially solves the atmospheric radiative transfer equation to find the amount of energy absorbed by the atmosphere across different angles. Although initially developed for the Earth's night sky, it has been field-tested with specialized earth simulators and actually provides more precise estimates of the amount of light scattered by particles in the air compared to common methods. Nonetheless, this approach does provide more accurate results when there is a clear view of the entire sky.

In complex environments, estimating a object's pose can be particularly challenging.  To address this, we introduce a novel technique, 'projection grouping', which leverages connected components derived from depth difference difference difference difference maps.  This method enhances the estimation of a object's pose by analyzing the relationship between component distributions and projected 3D model surfaces.  However, our approach relies on the assumption that at least part of the object in the scene is well-illuminated.  To mitigate this, we combine our projection grouping technique with an ancillary estimator, enabling us to both train and learn an illumination bias for each component, specifically tailored to its unique appearance.  Notably, our approach does not involve any form of illumination normalization.  Due to the sparse and scattered nature of available supervision, we utilize an elaborate graph structure to enable the exchange and propagation of pose information among multiple objects within the scene.  This design allows us to train an intricate multi-object pose estimator using depth difference maps derived from a single viewed example, as well as one another, and ultimately estimate the pose of any object in the scene.  To verify the effectiveness of our technique, we both trained and evaluated our model on the multi-object SUNPose100 dataset, as well as the single-object CMPose dataset.  Our findings show a notable improvement in pose estimation accuracy, with our method achieving an up to 25% improvement in HELEP health exercise equipment pose accuracy in comparison to the baseline depth

Peridynamic kernels are hypothesized to vary spatially, potentially contributing to the model's difficulty in predicting fractures. Through simulations of 1D and 21 problems, this study investigates this hypothesis and discovers that the kernel's inherent structure, characterized by distinct regions of 'soft', 'medium', and 'hard' regions, naturally tends to fail at the 'soft' region, minimizing the need for ad-hoc modifications to material properties. Furthermore, leveraging pre-existing kernel information can significantly reduce overfitting and overestimation of kernel modifications, ultimately demonstrating that fundamental changes in material properties are more likely to initiate fracture formation.

We enhance the Graphical Lasso framework by incorporating unobservable variables, as this allows a broader range of Gaussian graphical models and offers greater flexibility in modeling. By formulating an equivalent convex optimization problem, our proposed method leverages the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers to efficiently solve a previously non-convex objective function. Finally, on multiple real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our framework yields superior results compared to the standard Graphical Lasso and other popular model selection techniques.

This study compares two commonly used numerical techniques for solving the Fokker-Planck equation in molecular dynamics: implicit Euler and Verlet-Liouville leaf flooding. To validate our approach, our validations used benchmark solutions from prior research for the alanine dipeptide and protonated methionine dipeptide systems, as well as a test case based on a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator. Furthermore, our findings suggest that solving the periodic boundary condition problem using a Fourier series is more computationally efficient than using finite differences. Ultimately, our research indicates that the Verlet method outperforms the implicit Euler method under similar time step conditions, as well as during longer simulations.

This study explores the dynamics of binary black holes moving through a fluid environment, focusing on how initial configurations influence their movements. A numerical framework was developed to simulate the movement of two black holes within a fluid, using a second-order runge-kutta method for time-management and the spectral method for spatial approximations. The experiment was set in a square domain with cyclic boundaries, where binary black holes were placed at the center, moving horizontally, with opposing flows of fluid at the top and bottom boundaries. The results show that the initial conditions play a significant role in determining the binary black holes' trajectories, which can be either stable or unstable. In the case of unstable orbits, the binary black holes may become temporarily trapped in a circular area, or even fall out of synchronization and merge with each other. The merger can be triggered when the binary black holes are affected by a resonant interaction with the fluid's inertial waves.

This research investigates the long-term behavior of a system on a star-shaped graph whose branches have different lengths, extending from $1$ to $\infty$. Given an arbitrary, finite-based star graph with an associated $L^2$-type energy, we examine how elasticity on the graph's outer boundaries influence its boundary conditions. It has been established that when the graph contains more than one branch, boundary elasticity has a significant impact on the system's exponential stability. Specifically, when elasticity is absent on the graph's outer branches' boundaries, the boundary elastic module affects the boundary on the inner branches. Ultimately, this research has identified a condition, referred to as the "resonance avoidance" condition, and has demonstrated that it is sufficient to guarantee the system's exponential stability, and it is also a necessary condition in the absence of elasticity on the inner boundary.

Acoustic imaging techniques have been applied widely, yet they are limited by noise interference. A composite material called Stycast 1090SI has been proposed as an alternative to PMMA for use in acoustic imaging. This study aims to analyze the effects of Stycast 1090SI on the properties of acoustic waves and compare them to the impacts of PMMA. Experiments were conducted using two setups: one consisting of a water-PMMA-water arrangement, and the other containing water-Stycast 1090SI-water. Thicknesses of 10mm, 20mm, 30mm, 40mm, and 50mm were tested for both materials to investigate their effects. Results showed that Stycast 1090SI has similar acoustic properties to PMMA, albeit with lower attenuation levels. Although optimal central frequencies were observed for both materials, the frequency affected by the material could shift up to 50% of the original frequency. Moreover, the frequency spectrum affected by a 10mm thickness spans from 60% to 140% of the original frequency range, largely determined by the material's attenuation properties rather than its influence on wavelength. Overall, using a transducer array and advanced signal processing techniques can mitigate the effects of noise on the final images produced through acoustic imaging, making Stycast 1090SI a more suitable alternative to PMMA due to its improved

The analysis of dynamic processes across multiple time scales is a key aspect of understanding complex systems, with the use of a multilayer network providing a framework for this analysis. A critical issue in this context is how nodes within different network layers are interconnected, particularly when computing node centrality to identify their significance. Various techniques for computing centracity often rely on counting paths between nodes, which can be significantly impacted by the multilayer network's inter-layer connections. As a result, certain approaches to compute multilayer centrality must be developed taking into account the tendency of paths to deviate from specific nodes. This concept is operationalized through probability distributions that measure the likelihood of moving between different network layers. By doing so, a method proposing to compute multilayer betweenness centrality based on shortest paths is presented. This approach demonstrates how nodes within different network layers are connected through inter-layer links. A further analysis involving random multilayer networks reveals the influence of inter-layer links on multilayer betweenness centrality values. This study also highlights how different models for generating multilayer networks can have a substantial effect on centerness centrality values. A key aspect of this effect is the distinction between computing betweenness centrality for individual network layers versus the multilayer network as a whole. This difference is particularly pronounced in cases where nodes within different network layers possess the same basic properties. Recent astronomical photography utilizes color-dependent imaging sensors, enhancing overall clarity by correcting for the instrument's color sensitivity. A novel approach is presented, modifying RGB images through selective channel masking to optimize detail preservation. Four distinct strategies for RGB image correction are examined, utilizing benchmark images to evaluate performance. Results show a specific method, employing partial channel masking based on the formula $p_R = 0.5 \times p_G = 0.25 \times p_B$, to yield optimal outcomes. This technique outperforms alternative approaches in image quality, as evidenced by analysis using the SSIM similarity metric. A significant improvement of 0.1 in SSIM score is achieved, translating to roughly 10% better image quality.

A novel, formal approach is outlined to derive the Dirac equation within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, which is the spinor equivalent of the Minkowski spacetime through a conformal transformation. This method is then applied to obtain the Dirac equation within de Sitter spacetime, which is considered as a spacetime with intrinsic curvature derived from the $R$-Minkowski spacetime.

Structural causal models (SCMs) offer an abstract framework for depicting systems through variables and their interconnections, enabling a range of complex inferential calculations, such as estimating effects of interventions or predicting outcomes following such actions. A visual representation, called a directed graph, can effectively depict the relationships within an SCM's system. Although the 'pgm' R package provides comprehensive tools for probabilistic graphical models, it lacks the specificity to facilitate the development of complex causal models systematically. In contrast, the 'cdt' R package is now available to enable the systematic creation of such models, having implemented the equations of SCMs, their intervention versions, and associated graphs. A set of example scripts, included in the demonstration, shows how to model and analyze the classic "Titanic" dataset in the context of causal inference, integrating probabilistic and causal inference techniques from the 'pgm' and 'cdt' packages to estimate the effect of gender on survival rates following the ship's sinking.

This research delves into an internal cavity situated within a journal bearing, focusing on a rotating shaft and its interaction with the cavity's surface seal. As impact speeds rise, pressure inside the cavity drops, causing the seal to shift towards the bearing and potentially obstruct the oil supply to the main contact area. To address this challenge, a novel supply equation has been devised to track the seal's response and identify the threshold speed at which blockage occurs. Additionally, high-speed video recordings at various rotation rates have been utilized to validate experimental data, revealing that the seal may partially block the main contact region, thus influencing pressure buildup within the bearing.

Building upon a previous study, we explore how the generalized Witten effect restricts the energy spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity. By leveraging the generalized Witten effect and state-sum amplitudes from spin foams, we derive upper bounds for the number of charged black holes and extremal black holes with specific charges and masses within a given spin foam model. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the BPS property of states and their composite nature, comparing the BPS behavior of states analogous to the BCS coherence in superconductivity. In addition, we examine the impact of inserting Wilson loops on the spin foam amplitudes, showing how these insertions recover the Feynman amplitude for charged particles and provide upper bounds for linked Wilson loops with arbitrary holonomies.

Mobile applications are frequently collected for analysis, yet seldom are they subjected to comprehensive functional testing.
In contrast, researchers frequently examine shared libraries, identifying vulnerabilities and tweaking code to uncover security flaws.
However, examining the individual code components of applications that function independently is uncommon.
To address this limitation, we have developed a flexible operation system shell library, referred to as OctopOS, which emulates core Android functions for standalone applications.
Consequently, applications can be thoroughly tested without analysis modifications.
As an added advantage, we outline several cases where the code analysis can be skipped, allowing us to apply OctopAS directly to unmodified applications.
Moreover, we have conducted in-depth testing on unmodified applications utilizing OctopAS and discovered several unfound issues, as well as previously known security flaws, confirming the validity of our approach.

This research focuses on FPG (Filtered Policy Gradient), a variant of the PG algorithm that utilizes FPG estimators for efficient implementation in real-world applications. Corrupted episodes, where at least one state is altered during the episode, are a common occurrence. We have identified the vulnerability of standard PG to such occurrences and aimed to investigate whether FPG can provide a reliable learning guarantee, given that at most a single state is modified during each episode. A notable discovery emerged from our analysis: while the full PG algorithm fails to converge to an $\epsilon$-approximation of the optimal policy in scenarios with at most a single corrupted state, the FPG variant can achieve a $\epsilon$-approximation of the optimal policy within each episode, even with at most a single state being altered. To support our findings, we have established the limitations of policy updates and determined that reducing corruption to at most a single reward does not allow the FPG to reach a $\epsilon$-approximation of the optimal policy.

A solution has been proposed to the infamous "Quantum Paradox of the Mermin-Peres square" by identifying an underlying assumption in Peres' original argument. Peres' paradox, inspired by Bell's theorem and the "quantum paradox of the hat game," relies on a key concept known as "element of free choice" or "element of freedom" that was absent in Peres' initial analysis. According to a devised solution, a fundamental concept, referred to as "quantum element of surprise," must be incorporated into any viable solution to the paradox, along with the absence of a classical element of free choice. As a result, a redefined argument that excludes the element of freedom yields a contradiction, proving that an unbroken concept of freedom is a prerequisite to avoid the paradox's inconclusive outcome. Notably, a combined element, merging the concepts of freedom and surprise, can be seen as a dynamic aspect that governs a series of entanglement operations, often confused with a singular, monolithic concept. Lastly, the discussion is extended to address solutions to Peres' paradox that have been inconclusively derived, along with a solved variant of the paradox that mirrors the original "quantum hat game" and provides an explicable explanation.

Using first-principles electronic structure calculations and a Clifford algebra approach, we provide a thorough examination of the cubanite mineral. This analysis aims to address the mineral's geometric complications, apparent paradox of charge stability amidst diverse ion compositions, and explains its unusual ferromagnetic ordering. Firstly, we delve into the electronic structure of cubanite and its constituent parts, focusing on the spins aligned in the (001) plane. Next, we apply a 12-band model tailored to the (001) plane to investigate the (001) surface and compare it to experimental STS data. We discover that empty 3d states in cubanite contribute to its intrinsic ferro-magnetism, and that self-doped empty 4s states resolve the charge stability puzzle. Moreover, we identify that semi-filled 3d states on the (001) surface lead to conductivity anisotropy and potential topological surface states in cubanite.

The interaction between quantum dots and acoustic cavities offers a novel approach to controlling the dot's state and potentially performing logical operations.  By analyzing the dynamics of a quantum dot coupled to an acoustic cavity under the influence of an optical laser, it is possible to observe Rabi oscillations in the dot's population, a control mechanism whose effectiveness can be enhanced through changes in the driving frequency of the laser.  By mapping the time-dependent behavior of the Rabi oscillations to the frequency of the driving laser, more intuitive control over the dot's state is achieved.  Additionally, the acoustic cavity's properties such as the acoustic frequency and coupling strengths with the optical and electronic transitions have a measurable impact on the Rabi oscillations, which can be utilized to further refine the dot's state control through adjustments in these parameters.

A generalized Hamiltonian for the herringbone lattice has been examined through SPHINX, a versatile numerical method. The base Hamiltonian exhibits topological non-triviality, exhibiting a massless semimetal behavior with a distinct herringbone pattern. However, adding a simple perturbation to the Hamiltonian causes a crossover from this massless semimetal state to a massive semimetal state, characterized by an altered, periodic unit cell. To overcome these limitations, a thorough analysis was conducted to identify the topological properties of a broad class of SPHINX models, enabling a precise calculation of the SPHINC value for each. A key distinction between the massless and massive semimetal phases of the SPHINX lattice has been found, attributed to a difference in the SPHINC values, despite both possessing equivalent long-wavelength limits that determine their asymptotic, adsorbate-induced edge modes. Moreover, a thorough analysis was conducted to assess the robustness of the massless semimetal state, showcasing a resistance to a range of Hamiltonian perturbations that preserve a massless point-like semimetal characteristic. Although the massless semimetal state is relatively fragile, it can be harnessed to engineer chiral topological phases through a unitary similarity transformation, showcasing the potential of the SPHINX lattice as a novel, point-like topological model.

We achieve a higher success probability in producing single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) by combining a beam splitter and parametric amplifier, in contrast to the catalytic process using only a parametric amplifier or beam splitter individually. Notably, our proposed method requires fewer input resources yet produces SPCCSs with different parameters. Moreover, we demonstrate that beam splitter catalysis results in altered Gaussian fluctuations downstream compared to its parametric amplifier and coherent state input, in contrast to the Gaussian fluctuations induced by parametric amplifier catalysis. Furthermore, we show that beam splitter catalysis can also induce non-Gaussian fluctuations when considering its vacuum state and one-photon state equivalent input, in contrast to the coherent shift Gaussian fluctuations induced by vacuum state catalysis. We also provide a mathematical formula for calculating the success probabilities of our proposed two-input-resource-based catalytic process, and find that it differs from the single-input-resource-based catalytic process. Although our proposed method has lower success probabilities than the beam splitter vacuum-state catalytic process for expanding the Gaussian fluctuations, it has higher success probabilities for contracting the Gaussian fluctuations, which may be beneficial for generating squeezed states.

This paper provides a concise summary of key aspects of the complex Weyl tensor's
coefficients in the Newman-Penrose formalism, utilizing the Newman-Penrose
tetrad formalism. We offer a detailed explanation using Newman-Penrose formalism,
which involves four-vector bases and two-spinors, to derive the expressions for
$\Psi_{0}$ through $\Psi_{4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate the equivalence of
different formulations for $\Psi_{4}$, while previously, only expressions for
$\Psi_{0}$ and $\Psi_{4}$ had been presented in references like Teukolsky's
work.

Researchers have developed a new method for inferring the properties of polymers, an approach that utilizes an acyclic directed graph to represent the polymer based on its constituent monomers. This polymer representation captures interactions between remote monomers, which can mimic the effects of polymer growth. By connecting this structure to observations through a series of conditional probability distributions, the method can theoretically estimate the conditions necessary for a specific polymer configuration and the likelihood of observing certain characteristics. Unlike many existing methods that model each monomer independently, this model can also estimate the conditions required for multiple monomers to coexist. Consequently, the inferred conditions can be used to regulate the polymerization process. When evaluated on test samples, including DNA, this model proves effective in predicting polymer behavior and can be retrained with a target property to design new polymerization conditions.

This study explores the potential of using one ventilator to support multiple patients through distinct airway circuits, a technique that could be particularly valuable during ventilator shortages. A novel method is proposed, employing parallel ventilation setups that guarantee each patient receives their required air volume. The approach leverages positive pressure ventilation principles and adaptive flow controls to optimize outcomes. Key aspects such as the synchronization of ventilators and the influence of varying patient lung conditions are analyzed using a mathematical model. Computational simulations demonstrate how the proposed method effectively achieves accurate ventilation for each patient, and the findings provide valuable insights for clinical applications.

A critical step in radiotherapy treatment planning involves segmenting the esophagus, which can be complicated due to the modality and variability of the images. To address this challenge, a novel Deep Learning model, the Dilated Dense Attention Unet, has been developed for accurate esophageal tumor segmentation. To enhance feature extraction, dense connections have been incorporated into the UNet architecture, while an attention module, Dilated Dense UNet was found to produce superior results compared to the baseline UNet model. Experiments conducted on the public dataset from the MICCAI 2018 challenge demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed framework through various evaluations, ultimately achieving top-3 overall and top-5 segmentation results.

Recent machine learning form prediction models, particularly Long-term Memory Networks (LSTM), have been highly successful in real-world applications. However, their numerous memory cells and layers make them computationally intensive and time-consuming. Given the frequent forecasting tasks that require real-time processing, there is a pressing need to optimize these models for efficient implementation. We introduce a novel weight sharing technique, Non-overlapping Memory Cell Reutilization (MrML), to reduce the model's size and enhance formation evaluation efficiency. By implementing this strategy, we achieve a 90% decrease in memory cell count and a 90% improvement in real-time processing speed, with only minimal loss in prediction accuracy (less than 5%). We also introduce a dynamic memory adjustment strategy (DMrML) to further refine the model's performance by varying memory cells across input channels while maintaining real-time efficiency. We demonstrate that both MrML and DMrML exhibit superior performance compared to existing models, including support vector machines, random forest, and LSTM, in predicting well logs.

Our experiments demonstrate that adding background knowledge, such as context-independent information about language and world information, to our encoder allows for significant improvements in performance, with gains reaching up to 5.46% F-score. These enhancements come at a low computational cost and can even achieve similar results to the training set expansion method. Our results also suggest that our approach could potentially reduce the need for training data with high annotation costs, like coreference relations and verb phrases. We've designed our proposed method to be versatile and easily integratable into existing named entity recognition pipelines.

We employ Minassian's bitangent twist technique to analyze the rationality of bitangents in a specific, complicated quartic curve known as a tropical Jacobian. By approximating a complex mathematical object called a Monge-Ampere equation using free segment fitting, we attempt to handle the complexity introduced by a unique feature in the curve's edge structure. Our findings suggest that bitangents in this particular curve are inherently intertwined, making extraction of a smooth circle impossible without first resolving these complexities. Our work is a foundational study in using free segment fitting to manage and resolve complexities in rational approximation of real algebraic curves.

The proposed article presents a cutting-edge algorithm for estimating the two-dimensional location of events emitting impulsive signals, based on estimating a time difference of cross-correlation between pairs of microphones that detect those signals. Unlike traditional methods, this method does not require determining signal arrival times accurately, making it advantageous in situations with low sampling frequencies. A key innovation involves using an artificial neural network to map the received time differences directly to source locations, bypassing intermediate steps. Results from computer simulations and practical experiments demonstrate a high degree of accuracy, with errors averaging less than 5% of the distance from transducer to microphone. The neural network proves especially effective in scenarios where time differences are interrelated, allowing 100% increase in acceptable time interval spreads while maintaining high accuracy. The algorithm's robustness is highlighted with a substantial decrease in error rate compared to ideal conditions, while also showing resistance to noise interference.

which computer users can leverage to improve computer-human communication.
This field has made significant advancements, which has now permitted people to
obtain the advantages of advanced language understanding through computer
systems. Some key benefits include accessing education and work opportunities
for multilingual societies. While many languages have extensive resources
which facilitate effective improvements, this is not the case for lesser
resourced languages. Although state-of-the-art models such as BERT have
achieved remarkable success in well-resourced languages, their efficacy
significantly drops when applied to less-resourced languages. This is due to
two main factors such as dataset difficulty and model training data difficulty.
This field is crucial for research and has the potential to significantly
benefit multilingual societies. This paper researches state-of-the-art models
