A significant number of existing vision-based tools for accessing visual content rely on screen readers that use simple, often inaccurate descriptions. These systems' poor performance hampers the efficiency of visually impaired individuals in browsing online images. While current approaches to image description have achieved notable success, their outputs tend to be overly basic and full of errors. To enhance the reliability of screen reading software and improve its ability to convey visual information to users with impaired vision, it is crucial to establish standardized guidelines for the accurate and user-friendly generation of image descriptions. To facilitate this progress, a new dataset, iSUMM, has been created, consisting of high-quality, comprehensive descriptions that capture the essence of the content shown on the screens used to create the training data.

We investigate the electron energy loss function of three tantalum oxide phases namely Ta$_2$O$_5$, TaO$_2$ and TaO, focusing on the significance of local field corrections and spin-orbit coupling. Using time-dependent density functional theory within a bare Coulomb interaction model, we obtained computational results for both interband and intraband transitions across the tantalum oxides. To assess accuracy, our results were compared with experimental data for Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically electron energy loss spectroscopy and X-ray absorption spectroscopy. Our findings show that local field and spin-orbit considerations are crucial for computing energy loss functions, especially in TaO and TaO$_2$. Furthermore, our calculated intraband transitions for all three phases can be interpreted in terms of distinct optical properties. Notably, TaO and TaO$_2$ both exhibit good conductivity along their layered planes, with potential for carrier effective mass anisotropy.

A significant obstacle to comprehending the online dissemination of untruths lies in the growing segmentation of society into opposing groups, a tendency exacerbated by spatial isolation. We investigate how the non-linear, exponential expansion of geographical barriers hampers information transmission between remote areas. As a result, individuals in isolated regions may be exposed to untruths with delayed onset but increased prevalence. In contrast, online users experience a significantly accelerated rate of dissemination. Consequently, what we term 'The Big Sort' exerts a dominant influence on how untruths propagate, overshadowing the effects of other factors such as extreme content, endorsement from influential figures, or the inherent credibility of false claims. To illustrate this phenomenon in action, we explore how geographical isolation can shape the spread of untruths during a San Francisco earthquake and a COVID-19 lockdown in London.

Thanks to recent breakthroughs, annotation-costing attention mechanisms have achieved remarkable success across various domains. Nevertheless, their application has been limited due to the substantial computational requirements for training attention models on vast datasets. In response, this research develops an ultra-light attention model that functions as an plugin to the existing attention architecture, enabling it to be trained at minimal cost, computationally. Contrary to conventional approaches, this ultra-light attention module does not necessitate layer-by-layer processing, allowing it to be effectively utilized with existing annotations. Experimental evidence shows that an ultra-light attention module, despite being significantly more compact, equals or surpasses the performance of existing methods on vast datasets, with minimal annotation costs. Furthermore, it demonstrates flexibility in applying to various retrieval tasks, including multi-stage document, weakly supervised docu-paragraph, and end-to-end multi-task scenarios.

This research aims to analyze how varying conditions impact the underlying concepts
used in human language while instructing a partner on a complex task. We employed
a comprehensive dataset consisting of 1044 instances where humans teach each other
how to cook pasta on a multilingual platform. Through cooking demonstrations
categorized by language and methodical variation, we identified distinct patterns of
instructional variation. By examining these patterns in relation to core elements
such as key vocabulary, speech content, and cooking success rates, we identified
common concepts across diverse teaching scenarios. Our findings highlight that both
structural and semantic aspects of language vary freely while conveying core concepts
in speech, thereby supporting the validity of treating human feedback as context-
dependent, textual feedback in reinforcement learning.

This research focuses on the issue of identifying parents in ordered trees given their children information, extending the traditional parent-child to degree-parent problem. To address this extension, we explore how outdegree information can be utilized for parent specification, acknowledging that not all methods are effective. To resolve this, we introduce an innovative approach based on counterexample guidance for generating outdegree constraints that accurately define parent nodes in ordered trees. This approach stands out due to its flexibility in handling various types of ordered tree data without relying on specific characteristics, its user-friendly counterexample analysis for refining parent specifications, and its efficient use of available degree information. Our approach demonstrates its effectiveness through generated test cases, including a common scenario where initial parent specifications are incomplete due to missing outdegree details.

Inspired by Faddeev's recent remarks on the role of Euler-Arnold equations in closed open quantum field theory, we explore certain open Faddeev-Skyrme flux tube models based on a quadratic Dray-'Thorpe Hamiltonian. These models, which describe $SU(3)$ flux tubes with surface skyrme terms, exhibit nontrivial dynamics due to both bulk and boundary Skyrme terms. Our analysis reveals that the dynamics of these models can provide a foundation for understanding the $x$-dependence of the flux tube's wave functional, potentially addressing the problem of confinement in non-Abelian gauge theories. By applying a variational approach to the energy functional in the large $M$ limit, we demonstrate the effectiveness of a trial state built from the Dray-Thorme vacuum in capturing the desired properties of the flux tube. This trial state can be expressed in terms of the Euler-Arnold dynamics of a Lie algebra valued curve, where the resulting dynamics mirror those of an extended object living within the corresponding symmetric space.

Developing intelligent, interactive programs that can seamlessly interact with humans through natural language is an intricate and costly process. To facilitate the refinement of these programs during development, automated testing frameworks have been created to support continuous evaluation. Yet, a significant issue persists in the form of testing Frankenstein evaluations, a complex scenario where the user's input leads to an unexpected outcome based on the subsequent follow-up input and the resulting change in context. Current testing frameworks are limited in their capacity to handle the contextual shifts inherent in these scenarios. This challenge was addressed by the creation of a comprehensive suite of over 500 manual test cases and the establishment of a testing framework for conversational systems that can efficiently generate automated tests for complex situations. The newly proposed system, which was implemented in DiscoPipe, facilitates the use of Python for test specification and execution, addressing testing difficulties such as contextual changes. As a result, it now becomes possible to automate the evaluation of systems like chatbots and personal assistants, providing meaningful feedback on their performance.

Researchers are utilizing wide-field astrometric surveys, like Pan-STARRS1 and the Gaia mission, to identify invisible massive objects in our local cosmic neighborhood through the abnormal paths they create around solar system planets and dwarf stars. By utilizing sensitive astrometric measurements, these collaborations can pinpoint the locations and masses of such objects. In order to have a greater than 90% probability of discovering a new Earth-mass object via astrometry, the object should be located within 80 parsecs away. If micro-lensing is used, however, any object, regardless of its distance, can be found. Nevertheless, if it is located beyond 3000 parsecs, its gravitational pull will not significantly affect the movement of stars within our solar neighborhood. To increase the likelihood of finding a new Earth-mass object by micro-lensing, a sufficiently wide and deep survey, like the Gravitational Lens Survey Plus, with 280 million images, or an even more comprehensive survey, like the Gravitational Lens Survey Ultra, with 2.8 billion images, or even the LSST, with 10 billion images, or the Hyperia survey, with 100 billion images, or even more, with 1 trillion images, with 1000 million images, or even more, with 10000 million images, with 100000 million images, or even more, with 10

This work explores using memory-based techniques for machine translation between languages that have never been paired before. Specifically, we focus on a cross-lingual setting where three languages form a triangle (Language A to B to C), and we aim to translate from A to B despite only having paired data from B to A and A to C. We implement two approaches: one using monolingual memories (from A to B) and another using bi-directional memories (combining A to B and B to A). While the monolingual memory approach yields results comparable to strong bilingual membranes, the bi-directional memory strategy significantly outperforms them, showing up to a 12.5% improvement in translation quality. Furthermore, we introduce a innovative technique to create synthetic bi-directional memories through virtual translation of monolingual data, which proves effective in enhancing the model's performance.

The Planck satellite's observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) have confirmed the presence of "Hawking points"- a variance of $4\times 10^{-6}$ in temperature across specific low-variance circles in the sky. These features may arise from quantum fluctuations in the primordial universe influenced by black hole evaporation. Simulations using the ekpyrotic model, which involves the collision of two three-dimensional branes, have been able to reproduce the low-variance circles and the associated temperature anomalies. However, the ekpyrotic model fails to create sufficient primary black holes to account for the Hawking points. Secondary black holes, formed from the collision remnants, are found to produce smaller temperature variances than the observed values. Nevertheless, primary black holes with a mass of approximately $10^{15}$ grams are predicted to have evaporated by the time of recombination and could potentially be responsible for the Hawking points, even in conjunction with the effect of secondary black holes and a subsequent neutrino free-streaming phase. In this context, the temperature anomalies are localized due to the neutrino free-streaming phase reducing the influence of secondary black holes on the CMB temperature power spectrum from a global to a localized effect. Further analysis using Monte Carlo simulations confirms that the predicted temperature anomalies from primary and secondary black holes match the observations made by Planck. However, detecting these features while considering the full set of CMB anomalies is challenging. Notably, we

This study applies the technique of subsolutions and moving frames to examine a particular issue associated with the Yamabe flow for conformal metrics on a compact, positively curved compact manifold in high dimensions. Specifically, given a compact, n-dimensional (with n >= 3) manifold M and a function u in C^2(M), the given condition leads to a transformation where the scalar curvature of the resulting metric satisfies a specific equation, where |R| power p is denoted as v and V is a function involving the derivative of a given, smooth, convex function f with respect to its first argument.

In various scenarios, this problem has been shown to admit a unique solution over an infinite time period, a locally defined unique solution, multiple distinct solutions, or only non-constant solutions under specific initial conditions.

Our framework provides a versatile solution for optimizing few-shot learning by learning contrastive representations under limited supervision, a solution that tackles the common problem of contamination by abnormal samples. Our method tackles this challenge by initially filtering unusual samples through the k-nearest neighbor algorithm within the metric space, a common retrieval technique. Furthermore, our framework employs a contrastive learning approach to differentiate normal samples, a common representation method. Our model is controllable through the framework, a key feature of our framework.

User preference is an essential yet frequently ignored component in recommendation systems. Existing models that incorporate user preference are often limited by basic or inefficient methods of utilization. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new framework called Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) that focuses on two key aspects: aspect-level preference extraction and aspect-level preference preference enhancement. GAPE employs an adaptable preference encoder to capture user preference across various aspects, generating context-dependent representations for any given aspect. Moreover, GAPE employs the Attention-gated enhancement encoder to efficiently integrate aspect-level preferences, resulting in more accurate representations. We have conducted comprehensive experiments on three public datasets, and the results show significant performance gains, surpassing 10% in some cases compared to state-of-the-art methods. GAPE's versatility allows it to be applied to both point-of-interest recommendation and e-commerce recommendation, and open-source implementations of our code and models are available online.

This paper presents nature-inspired formulations that mimic the effectiveness of state-of-the-art extended formulations, offering a significantly lower dimensional representation. We demonstrate this concept by formulating exotic cones of limited dimension that approximate or equal well-known cones such as the second-order cone, non-negative reals, and binary values. These unusual cones can be integrated into broader formulations, replacing standard representations and yielding compact models for commonly used optimization problems like network design, bin packing, knapsack problem, and cutting stock. These formulations suggest that complex extended formulations may be achievable through simple applications of appropriate cone formulations.

Deep learning technology has significantly progressed over the last decade, notably in the field of medical image analysis, where models now outperform many radiologists in certain tasks. However, there are concerns regarding their ability to generalize to new, unseen data. Assessing model performance on previously unseen datasets is crucial for ensuring their reliability in clinical applications. This study applies a rigorous evaluation framework from computer science to evaluate computer-assisted dementia detection models trained on unpooled MRI data against models trained on aggregated datasets. Evaluating these models on datasets they have not encountered during training demonstrates that dementia prediction models trained on unassociated MRI scans were less accurate than those trained on a consolidated dataset. This discrepancy suggests that the specific composition of the training dataset has a significant impact on model performance, especially when they are trained on data from the same source. Furthermore, it emphasizes the critical importance of assessing computer-assisted medical analysis models on datasets they have not encountered during training to ensure their effectiveness and accuracy in a clinical setting.

This paper proposes a framework for network-based optimization problems that involves a network of interacting decision variables, each associated with an objective and a set of interaction costs. We explore two approaches: forming a differentiable network that can be optimized as a whole, and a framework of network-based optimization problems. The proposed solutions can be applied by redefining specific components, such as a distance function and interaction sets. We also propose a frame of reference that can be used to develop efficient optimization techniques, such as a descent algorithm. This framework can be applied to various problems, such as embedding problems and finding optimal synchronizations.

Researchers have investigated the performance of various Optane DC PMM file systems, including NOVA in its relaxed and enforced modes, finding significant improvements in performance compared to the original SSD file system. Specifically, around a 10x gain was seen for relaxed writes and an even greater performance increase of approximately 20x was observed for I/O-bound applications like MongoDB, which involve less frequent disk writes. Nevertheless, this 10x performance boost for relaxed writes comes with the risk of unlogged writes leading to potential data corruption upon sudden power failure. Nevertheless, NoVA delivers an order of magnitude better performance than optane-ssd for I/O-bound applications, which involve fewer disk writes.

Andriy Suslov's thesis explores the motivation-driven approach to biologically-inspired swarm intelligence and delves into a novel multi-agent system called eMD. This framework, an advancement of the Motivation Dynamics model, showcases effective and stable rendezvous interactions, showcasing two distinct agent types with unique goals that lead to collaborative behavior. Through a theoretical analysis, the conditions for successful meeting are established, demonstrating how contrasting drives facilitate the rendezvous process. Furthermore, real-world experiments using Raspberry Pi 3 devices validate the capabilities of the eMD algorithm.

Our study focuses on the magnetic properties of the intermetallic hexagonal alloys GdxCm1-xSn3, which belong to the rare-earth metals family and have the AuCu3 crystal structure. Using specific heat measurements, we analyzed how these compounds respond to changes in temperature and also examined their responses to changes in a magnetic field. Our findings demonstrate a significant variation in the magnetic moment within the CmxGdxSn3 compounds, influenced by the Cm concentration. Notably, the maximum magnetic moment was observed at x = 0.3, indicating that the hybridization of the 5f electrons of Cm with the Sn p-electrons plays a crucial role in shaping the magnetic behavior. This effect gives rise to various phenomena, including an anti-Ce-like Kondo effect. Our theoretical calculations utilizing the Anderson Hamiltonian in conjunction with a microscopic approach to the f-electron hybridization further substantiate our observations.

The properties of heavy quarkonia, such as charmonium and bottomonium, are dominated by the strong force interactions between quarks, which result in bound states. Calculating these interactions via Lattice QCD simulations requires understanding the quark-antiquark potential, with the static case being representable as an effective potential model with minimal parameters. For dynamic quark pairs, the situation is complicated, calling for multiple effective descriptions with varying ranges of application. This study presents an approach to unify these frameworks through the Hadron Level Lattice Action, facilitating calculations of bound state properties across the entire mass spectrum. The method is tested on the QCD lattice to produce diverse spectra, and in comparison with experimental observations, it demonstrates accuracy for both static and dynamic cases. The effective Lagrangian parameters are further refined using a global fit, and the outcome is showcased on a comprehensive set of spectra, demonstrating the viability of the hadron level action in modeling the full spectrum of charmonium states.

Using the approach developed for symmetric groups, we extend this to Coxeter groups of type Bn by redefining the standard descent set to include the position of the 0 in one-based indexing. The revised generalized standard expressions (OGS) for type Bn then aligns with those for the symmetric group Sn. Additionally, we establish exchange rules for the generalized standard expressions of type Bn by showing how the generalized stroganov expressions for the symmetric group Sn serve as a subset of the Coxeter group Bn. The exchange rules demonstrate how dividing a generalized standard expression by the rightmost generator results in another generalized standard expression, while multiplying by a different generator requires inserting it into the expression at a specific position. Furthermore, we establish connections between OG elements with high descent values and those with lower descent values through generalized standard expressions.

A comprehensive set of 12 halo properties is examined within a range of $10^9.5$ to $10^{11.5}$ solar masses for the halo mass and $800$ to $8000$ km/s for the halo velocity, focusing on the gravitational potential, dark matter distribution, stellar content, cosmic ray influence, particle accretion history, satellite galaxy count, shape, rotation, and tidal effects. A theoretical framework combining numerical simulations, analytical models, and empirical relationships is developed to predict these halo properties and is validated through comparisons with various observations and independent theoretical sources. Constraints imposed by this validation process are used to refine relevant parameters within the underlying theoretical framework known as $\Lambda$CDM. Furthermore, an efficient implementation of this model in Python is made available to facilitate future research.

This paper presents a new framework for Holley-Stone calculus, based on the Boolean-valued approach. The main theoretical framework is established first for a discrete case, involving two operators defined over a Boolean-valued $L^2$ space derived from a finite measure defined on a power-set. The framework is then extended to a stochastic setting, utilizing a Brownian motion-valued measure defined over a Boolean-valued $\sigma$-algebra.

The primary obstacle in realizing the T centre in silicon carbone for quantum applications lies in resolving its extremely narrow spin-resolved fluorescence at 812 nm. Initially, researchers studied the T centre within 6 eV UV-damaged silicon carbone (UCSiC), but this method was limited by available UV lasers. In contrast, this research demonstrates that high-quality bulk silicon carbone enables UCSiC-like damage and preserves the T centre under visible light laser excitation. Although there is a 0.55 eV red-shift in the T centre's valence band position in UV-damaged regions compared to silicon carbone, researchers successfully observed the T centre in silicon carbone, with similar spin-resolved features as in UV-damaged silicon carbone. However, Si-doped silicon carbone proved unsuitable as it shifts the T centre to lower energies, making it impossible to observe the desired spin-dependent fluorescence. By enhancing the UV damage and confining the T centre to the damage layer, researchers managed to increase the spin sensitivity of the fluorescence. This indicates that with optimized silicon carbone samples, quantum technologies based on the T centre become feasible.

This paper outlines three techniques for tumor identification in CT scans, namely Morphological Tools, Region Growing Technique, and a combination of both. The first section provides an overview of the selected methods, while the second section evaluates each technique based on multiple factors, ultimately recommending the most effective one.

In this study, we aim to provide a clearer understanding of the degenerate Bernoulli numbers first introduced by Kim and Kim in 2012. By leveraging a matrix-based approach to these numbers, we demonstrate their equivalence to a specific determinant associated with de Moivre's matrix, which was also previously examined by Kim and Kim. This alternative proof of their calculation is rather straightforward and offers a simpler method than the previously established proof. Additionally, we explore the connection between degenerate Bernoulli numbers and Circulant matrices over Galois fields to project calculations of de Moivre's matrix determinant over these fields. This relationship not only aids in understanding the computation of these numbers but also enables us to determine their values modulo prime numbers. This relationship demonstrates the interplay between discrete mathematics and linear algebra, highlighting how such concepts can be utilized together to solve complex problems.

The ultimate goal of precise astrometry is to minimize radial velocity fluctuations caused by the presence of exoplanets within a star system. Although various line-list selection strategies have been explored, including optimized, manual, and simplified methods, their effectiveness is yet to be thoroughly compared. In this study, a novel approach called random selection was implemented to evaluate the performance of different line-list methods. A dataset consisting of over 5 million spectral features was analyzed to assess how each selection strategy affects radial velocity jitter. Unlike previous studies that focused on a limited set of spectral lines, our analysis involves a large dataset and thoroughly models systematic noise. We simulated observations of a typical M dwarf star, comparing the performance of different line-lists in reducing radial velocity jitter, specifically evaluating a randomized selection approach against traditional methods. Our results indicate that a randomized approach yields similar outcomes to a traditional method, suggesting that a comprehensive spectrum of spectral features is more critical than carefullychoosing a specific subset. Furthermore, a novel data structure was developed to facilitate efficient cross-correlation of spectra against massive spectral templates, significantly speeding up analysis time. When tested on a commodity server, this algorithm demonstrated a substantial increase in processing speed, exhibiting linear scalability and improved performance on larger spectra.

We investigate designing low-energy scheduling for wireless sensor networks while minimizing sleep time and preventing collisions. A hierarchical method called Range Sectoring is proposed, dividing the network into sectors at different energy levels. RTS/CTS frames are used to identify suitable time slots for data transmission within each sector. A hierarchical structure reduces the 'hidden terminal' problem by limiting the range of CTS transmission. A central coordinator manages SCST protocols at each level to minimize end-to-latency. A simulation study evaluates the effectiveness of Range Sectoring, demonstrating significant reductions in total energy consumption and latency compared to AODV in wireless sensor networks.

A universally accepted solution for identifying objects in images does not exist,  
as suitable methods vary by context. This is particularly true for scenarios  
involving image analysis with embedded systems, where performance constraints are tight.  
Current approaches using Flask servers are not appropriate in this case, given the  
latency and cost associated with them. This study investigates the use of lightweight  
and low-cost object detectors, tailored for computing environments restricted to  
raspberry pi devices. Various detectors were assessed based on such criteria as  
accuracy, processing speed, and optimal usage cases. For our experiments, we focused  
on the use cases involving real-time processing on single-image inputs on raspberry pi  
hardware. Yet, the experiment framework presented can easily be adapted for other  
scenarios, simply by altering the relevant parameters in the existing code.

This paper focuses on a specific type of elliptic system and investigates its properties. The system involves functions that grow at different rates in specific regions, and we establish conditions for the system to have solutions under certain circumstances. We prove that if a key function remains bounded, it guarantees the presence of large solution components for certain parameter values and also yields new result in regard to partially positive solution when another function grows at a slower rate, it guarantees the systems' ability to have solution, ultimately, these findings contribute to a broader understanding of elliptic systems with diverse growth characteristics, and an example is provided to illustrate the applicability of the theoretical framework developed in this study, and and a side note in regard to previous research on systems with monotonic functions.

This study seeks to improve existing bounds for the variance of functions related to independent Bernoulli random variables when they are conditioned upon their sum. As a result, specific concentration results can be derived for convex functions, polynomials, and smooth non-convex functions within this context. as well as insights into the large deviation probability of such conditioned Bernoulli sums. Some of the findings relate to the distribution characteristics of certain random variables representing the number of edges and triangles in random graphs, as well as insights into the behavior of Bernoulli sums with fixed edge counts.

This article presents new comparisons between étale and crystalline cohomology for a smooth projective scheme over a $p$-adic integer ring. An analogue of the Fundamental Exact Sequence is established, linking torsion crystalline cohomology, étale cohomology, and extensions between them for a smooth projective scheme in characteristic zero. Additionally, we generalize a previous result regarding the connection between étale and crystalline cohomology in characteristic zero.

We explore the possibility of measuring the $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry in semi-inclusive single-hadron production to increase our understanding of the dihadron fragmentation function (DiFF). This process involves a heavy quark undergoing deep inelastic scattering and emitting a hard gluon before emitting a hadron. Calculations of the cross section include leading twist terms and T-odd asymmetry arising from the interference between cut diagonal quark-gluon correlations. We also examine how finite-c$_t$ effects influence the cross section, specifically looking at central and forward rapidity regions, and identify the optimal conditions for measuring the $p T$ dependence of the $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry at the FCC-eh.

Using the Fock transformation, we've developed a coherent 'clock' that can measure invariant elapsed time within de Sitter spacetime, a concept also relevant to Minkowskian spacetime. This clock is founded on the generation invarisante length, which remains unchanged within de Sitter spacetime, a fundamental aspect of its associated group, $SO(4,2)$. This framework enables us to derive the de Sitter spacetime framework from the Minkowskian one, a significant finding given our established understanding of Minkowskian spacetime. Consequently, we can now frame the de Sitter spacetime framework as an extension of the Minkowskian one, a conclusion that challenges the prevailing view on vacuum energy. This new perspective allows us to determine the de Sitter spacetime framework through the Minkowskian one, a significant finding with broader implications. As a direct outcome, we can now express the de Sitter spacetime framework in terms of the Minkowskian one, a significant finding with implications for vacuum energy. This new perspective enables us to view the de Sitter spacetime framework through the lens of the Minkowskian one, a significant finding with profound consequences. This framework facilitates a unified understanding of the de Sitter and Minkowskian spacetime frameworks, a significant finding with potential effects on our comprehension of the cosmos.
